title: Lab: handling a security incident end to end
summary: Work a realistic incident from first alert to lessons learned: a phishing-driven credential theft and suspicious PowerShell on a managed endpoint. You will triage in Defender XDR, scope with advanced hunting, contain, eradicate, recover and harden, integrating everything from this month.
objectives: Triage a multi-stage Defender XDR incident by correlating identity and endpoint alerts into one timeline
Scope the blast radius with an advanced hunting KQL query joining sign-in and device process telemetry
Contain the threat by isolating the device, revoking sessions and disabling the account, leaning on Conditional Access and CAE
Eradicate persistence and rotate credentials and secrets the attacker may have touched
Recover the endpoint and user safely while verifying BitLocker and compliance state
Run a post-incident review and close the root-cause gap with a new Conditional Access policy or ASR rule

quiz.q: A Defender XDR incident links a risky sign-in from an impossible-travel location to a 'Suspicious PowerShell download' alert on a managed laptop. What is the single best first action during triage?
options: Open the incident, read the correlated alert story and build a timeline before acting
Immediately re-image the laptop before looking at anything else
Email the user to ask if they ran PowerShell
Delete the user's mailbox to stop data loss
quiz.why: Defender XDR already correlates identity and endpoint alerts into one incident with an attack story; reading that timeline first prevents premature, destructive actions and tells you exactly what to contain. Re-imaging or deleting data first destroys evidence and may not even address the root cause.

quiz.q: You want to scope how far the compromised account spread. Which advanced hunting approach is most effective?
options: Search only DeviceProcessEvents on the one known device
Join identity sign-in events with device process and network events across the tenant by account and time window
Query AlertInfo alone and trust the alert count
Run a full antivirus scan and read the log
quiz.why: Scoping means following the account and indicators across all telemetry. Joining sign-in logs (AADSignInEventsBeta / SigninLogs) with DeviceProcessEvents and DeviceNetworkEvents by the compromised UPN and time window reveals other devices, IPs and processes the attacker touched — far more than a single-device or single-table query.

quiz.q: During containment you isolate the device in Defender for Endpoint and disable the account in Entra. Why also explicitly revoke the user's sessions?
options: Disabling an account instantly kills all existing tokens everywhere
Existing access and refresh tokens can remain valid until expiry unless revoked; revocation plus CAE forces re-auth in near real time
Revoking sessions restores the deleted files
quiz.why: Disabling the account stops new sign-ins, but already-issued tokens may stay valid up to their lifetime. Revoking sessions invalidates refresh tokens, and Continuous Access Evaluation propagates the change to resources in near real time, closing the window an attacker could keep using a live session.

quiz.q: After eradication you are ready to recover. Which check confirms the endpoint is safe to release from isolation and return to the user?
options: The user says the laptop 'feels fine'
The antivirus definitions are up to date
No active EDR detections, persistence removed, credentials rotated, and the device reports compliant and BitLocker-protected
quiz.why: Recovery is gated on verified clean state: no live detections, removed persistence, rotated secrets, and a confirmed compliant, encrypted device. Subjective impressions or a single signal like AV definitions are not sufficient evidence that the threat is gone.

quiz.q: In your own words, why is correlating the identity signal (risky sign-in) with the endpoint signal (suspicious process) more powerful than treating each alert alone?
quiz.answer: Alone, a risky sign-in might look like a false positive and a suspicious process might look like benign admin activity; correlated, they form a clear attack story — stolen credentials being used to run malicious code on a real device — which raises confidence, defines scope, and tells you to contain both the identity and the endpoint together.
quiz.why: XDR's value is breadth across domains. Correlation turns two ambiguous low-confidence signals into one high-confidence incident, drives the right containment on both the account and the device, and reveals lateral movement a single-domain view would miss.

quiz.q: Name one root-cause hardening control you would add in the post-incident review for a phishing-to-token-theft incident, and say which principle it enforces.
quiz.answer: Add a Conditional Access policy requiring phishing-resistant MFA and a compliant device for the affected app, optionally with token protection / sign-in frequency; this enforces 'verify explicitly' and least privilege so stolen passwords alone cannot grant access. An ASR rule blocking script-launched executables or credential theft from LSASS is an equally valid endpoint-side answer.
quiz.why: Post-incident hardening must close the gap the attacker used. Phishing-resistant MFA plus device compliance defeats password-only and many token-replay attacks, while ASR rules cut off the script-based execution chain — both directly map to Zero Trust principles taught this month.

body_markdown:
## The scenario

It is 09:14 on a Tuesday. A **Defender XDR** incident lights up your queue, severity High, correlating two alerts: a **risky sign-in** for `j.okafor@contoso.com` from an unfamiliar IP flagged *impossible travel*, and a *Suspicious PowerShell download activity* alert on her managed laptop `LT-OKAFOR-01`. The attack story writes itself: a **phishing** email harvested her credentials, the attacker signed in, and a **LOLBin** PowerShell one-liner pulled a payload onto the endpoint. This is your capstone — you will run the full **IR lifecycle** (NIST SP 800-61: *prepare, detect & analyse, contain, eradicate & recover, post-incident*) using every control from this month.

## Detect and analyse: read the story, then scope

Open the incident and read the correlated timeline **before touching anything**. XDR has already joined the identity and endpoint signals for you — confirm the **IOC**s: the source IP, the spawned process, any outbound C2 domain. Then scope the blast radius with **advanced hunting**. Do not trust a single device or single table; follow the account across the tenant:

```kql
let target = "j.okafor@contoso.com";
let window = 24h;
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where Timestamp > ago(window) and AccountUpn == target
| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("high", "medium")
| project Timestamp, IPAddress, Country, DeviceName, Application
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(window)
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("powershell.exe", "cmd.exe", "mshta.exe")
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DownloadString", "-enc", "Invoke-WebRequest")
    | project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl=InitiatingProcessRemoteSessionDeviceName
) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp asc
```

This tells you which **devices**, IPs and processes the one compromised identity touched — your true scope.

## Contain: cut access on both the identity and the endpoint

Containment is two-sided because this is an XDR incident. On the **endpoint**, isolate the device so it keeps its EDR link but loses everything else:

```powershell
# From a SOC workstation using the Defender for Endpoint API / portal action:
# 1) Device > Isolate device (Full)  -> severs network, keeps Defender comms
# 2) Identity side, in Entra / Graph PowerShell:
Update-MgUser -UserId "j.okafor@contoso.com" -AccountEnabled:$false
Revoke-MgUserSignInSession -UserId "j.okafor@contoso.com"
```

Disabling the account stops new sign-ins; **revoking sessions** invalidates refresh tokens; and because **Continuous Access Evaluation (CAE)** is on, those revocations propagate to resources in near real time rather than waiting for token expiry. Your existing **Conditional Access** posture is what made the device isolatable and the account governable in the first place.

## Eradicate and recover

**Eradicate** the foothold: remove the dropped payload and any **persistence** (scheduled task, Run key, new service), then rotate everything the attacker may have seen — reset the user's password, rotate any app secrets or keys cached on the device, and review **PKI** certificates that may need revoking. **Recover** only on verified-clean evidence: no live EDR detections, persistence gone, and the device reporting **compliant** with **BitLocker** protection healthy. Then release the device from isolation, re-enable the account behind a fresh **MFA** challenge, and restore access.

## Post-incident: close the gap

The incident is not over until the **root cause** is fixed. The attacker won with a phished password and password-only access. So harden: add a **Conditional Access** policy requiring **phishing-resistant MFA** and a compliant device for sensitive apps, and add an **ASR rule** to block script-launched executables. Write up the timeline, the dwell time, and what detection or control would have caught it sooner.

## Your task

In a test tenant, simulate this incident end to end. (1) Generate or locate a risky sign-in plus a suspicious PowerShell event so a correlated XDR incident appears. (2) Triage it and write a one-page timeline of the attack story. (3) Run an advanced hunting query (adapt the KQL above) to scope which devices and accounts were affected, and paste the results. (4) Contain: isolate the device, disable the account and revoke sessions, noting how CAE behaves. (5) Eradicate and recover: remove persistence, rotate the password, verify compliance and BitLocker, then release isolation. (6) Deliver a post-incident report naming one new Conditional Access policy AND one ASR rule you would deploy, and which Zero Trust principle each enforces.

slides.title: Lab: handling a security incident end to end
slides.sub: Month 3 - Advanced Endpoint Security & Identity  |  Lesson 8
slides.narration: Welcome to the capstone lab for Month Three. Everything we've built this month — Zero Trust, Conditional Access, Defender and advanced hunting, E D R and incident response, hybrid identity, P K I and BitLocker — comes together now. We're going to work one realistic incident from the very first alert all the way through to lessons learned. By the end you'll have run the full incident response lifecycle on a managed endpoint, and you'll finish with a hands-on lab that ties the whole month together.

slides.title: The scenario
bullets: High-severity Defender X D R incident hits your queue.
A risky sign-in for one user from an impossible-travel IP.
A suspicious PowerShell download on her managed laptop.
Story: phishing stole creds, then code ran on the device.
slides.narration: Here's our scenario. It's nine fourteen on a Tuesday and a Defender X D R incident lights up your queue at high severity. It correlates two things: a risky sign-in for Jane Okafor from an unfamiliar I P flagged as impossible travel, and a suspicious PowerShell download alert on her managed laptop. The story almost writes itself — a phishing email harvested her credentials, the attacker signed in, and a living-off-the-land PowerShell command pulled a payload onto the endpoint. This is exactly the kind of multi-stage incident X D R was built to catch.

slides.title: The IR lifecycle (NIST 800-61)
bullets: Prepare — controls and tooling already in place.
Detect & analyse — read the story, confirm IOCs.
Contain, then eradicate & recover.
Post-incident — learn and harden the root cause.
slides.narration: We'll follow the incident response lifecycle from NIST eight hundred sixty-one. Prepare, which is everything we set up earlier this month. Detect and analyse, where we read the attack story and confirm the indicators of compromise. Contain, to stop the bleeding. Eradicate and recover, to remove the threat and safely restore. And finally post-incident, where we capture lessons learned and harden so it can't happen the same way again. Notice that response is a disciplined sequence, not a panic.

slides.title: Detect & analyse: read first
bullets: Open the incident; read the correlated timeline first.
X D R already joined identity and endpoint alerts.
Confirm IOCs: source IP, process, any C2 domain.
Do not act destructively before you understand it.
slides.narration: The first discipline is to read before you act. Open the incident and study the correlated timeline. Defender X D R has already stitched the identity alert and the endpoint alert into a single attack story for you — that's the whole point of X D R. Confirm your indicators of compromise: the source I P, the process that spawned, any command-and-control domain. The biggest rookie mistake here is to re-image or delete something immediately. Understand the story first, because premature action destroys the evidence you need to scope it.

slides.title: Scope with advanced hunting
bullets: Follow the account across the whole tenant.
Join sign-in events with device process events.
One device or one table is never enough scope.
The query reveals every device and IP the attacker touched.
slides.code:
let target = "j.okafor@contoso.com";
AADSignInEventsBeta
| where AccountUpn == target
| where RiskLevelDuringSignIn in ("high","medium")
| join kind=leftouter (
    DeviceProcessEvents
    | where InitiatingProcessFileName == "powershell.exe"
    | where ProcessCommandLine has_any
        ("DownloadString","-enc")
) on DeviceName
| order by Timestamp asc
slides.narration: Now we scope the blast radius with advanced hunting in K Q L. The key insight is to follow the compromised account across the entire tenant, not just the one device you already know about. So we take the risky sign-in events for that user and join them to device process events where PowerShell ran something suspicious — a download string, an encoded command. That join tells us every device, every I P and every process this one stolen identity touched. That's your true scope, and it's almost always bigger than the single alert suggested.

slides.title: Contain the identity
bullets: Disable the account to stop new sign-ins.
Revoke sessions to kill existing refresh tokens.
CAE propagates revocation in near real time.
Conditional Access made the account governable.
slides.narration: Containment is two-sided in an X D R incident. Start with the identity. Disabling the account stops new sign-ins, but here's the subtlety: already-issued tokens can stay valid until they expire. So you must also revoke the user's sessions, which invalidates the refresh tokens. And because Continuous Access Evaluation is switched on, that revocation propagates out to the resources in near real time instead of waiting up to an hour. This is exactly the Conditional Access and C A E machinery we built earlier this month, now earning its keep.

slides.title: Contain the endpoint
bullets: Isolate the device in Defender for Endpoint.
Full isolation severs network but keeps EDR comms.
You can still investigate and run live response.
Both halves contained — identity and device together.
slides.code:
Defender portal:
  Device > Isolate device (Full)
  -> network severed, Defender link kept
slides.narration: Now the endpoint half. In Defender for Endpoint you isolate the device, and you choose full isolation. This severs the device from the network so the attacker loses their channel, but it deliberately keeps the Defender communication link alive so you can still investigate and run live response on it. Isolate the device and contain the identity together — that's the discipline. Cutting only one half leaves the attacker a path, whether that's a live token or a live network connection.

slides.title: Eradicate & recover
bullets: Remove the payload and any persistence mechanism.
Rotate creds: password, app secrets, PKI certs as needed.
Recover only on verified-clean evidence.
Confirm compliant + BitLocker healthy before release.
slides.narration: With the threat contained we eradicate the foothold. Remove the dropped payload and hunt down any persistence — a scheduled task, a Run key, a sneaky new service. Then rotate everything the attacker might have seen: reset the user's password, rotate any app secrets or keys cached on that device, and review whether any P K I certificates need revoking. Only then do we recover, and only on verified-clean evidence — no live detections, persistence gone, the device reporting compliant and BitLocker protection healthy. Then, and only then, release the device from isolation and re-enable the account behind a fresh M F A challenge.

slides.title: Post-incident: close the gap
bullets: The incident isn't over until root cause is fixed.
Attacker won with a phished, password-only login.
Add CA: phishing-resistant MFA + compliant device.
Add an ASR rule to block script-launched executables.
slides.code:
Hardening to deploy:
  CA policy -> require phishing-resistant MFA
               + compliant device on the app
  ASR rule -> block executable content from
              script (LOLBin chain)
slides.narration: The incident isn't finished when the device is clean — it's finished when the root cause is closed. Our attacker won with a phished password and password-only access. So we harden. Add a Conditional Access policy that requires phishing-resistant M F A and a compliant device for the sensitive app, which enforces verify explicitly. And add an attack surface reduction rule to block executable content launched from scripts, which breaks the living-off-the-land chain on the endpoint. Then write up the timeline, the dwell time, and what would have caught it sooner.

slides.title: Recap & your lab task
bullets: The month converges: Zero Trust, CA, XDR, EDR, identity, PKI, BitLocker.
Lifecycle: detect, scope, contain both sides, eradicate, recover, harden.
Correlation turns weak signals into one strong incident.
Task: run this incident end to end and deliver a post-incident report.
slides.narration: Let's recap the whole month converging here. Zero Trust gave us the mindset, Conditional Access and C A E gave us the controls, Defender X D R and advanced hunting gave us detection and scope, E D R gave us isolation and live response, hybrid identity, P K I and BitLocker gave us the recovery checks. The lifecycle is: detect and analyse, scope with K Q L, contain both the identity and the device, eradicate persistence, recover on clean evidence, then harden the root cause. Your lab task: in a test tenant, simulate this incident end to end. Trigger a correlated X D R incident, write a one-page attack timeline, scope it with an advanced hunting query and paste the results, contain by isolating the device and revoking sessions, eradicate and recover while verifying compliance and BitLocker, and finally deliver a post-incident report naming one new Conditional Access policy and one A S R rule you'd deploy — and which Zero Trust principle each one enforces. That's the capstone. Well done on Month Three.
